name: Bariba / Batonu
confidence_why: Welmers 1952, from fieldwork at Nikki, describes Bariba as a tone language with four level tones plus rising and falling and never mentions stress, and the only possible dissent is Westermann's 1922 sketch from a single speaker, whose wording ('Starkton' on the stem syllable) belongs to a period when such remarks usually stood for what later work analysed as tone.
catalog_citation: Welmers, William E. 1952. Notes on the structure of Bariba. Language 28(1): 82-103. DOI 10.2307/409991 (open archive.org scan of the Kraus 1964 reprint of Language vol. 28, item).
catalog_quote: Tones (illustrated on the vowel a): top /á/, high /a/, mid /ā/, low /à/, falling /â/, rising /ǎ/. [p. 83] ... Both final and preconsonantal /m, n/ are always syllabic and have a tone; unmarked final or preconsonantal /m, n/ have high tone. [p. 84] ... Each tone is found in contrast with at least three others, and most of them with all five others. [p. 85] ... Rising and falling tones are rather rare. Rising tone occurs in a few morphemes, but not in any noun or verb stem. It is often the result of the addition of a morpheme with another alternant consisting of a syllable with high tone. Falling tone occurs with a few verb stems, and also as the result of the addition of a morpheme with another alternant consisting of a syllable with low tone. [p. 86] ... In this study, word division is written arbitrarily. There is no immediately apparent evidence of other phonemic junctures. [p. 86 fn. 7] ... A series of one or more high tones at the end of a word becomes mid after low at the end of a sentence [p. 87]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bariba is described purely as a tone language: four contrastive level tones (top, high, mid, low) plus falling and rising contours, borne by every syllable including syllabic nasals; extensive tone sandhi (e.g. word-final high tones become mid after low at the end of a sentence). Welmers never mentions stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the 22-page description, so no word-stress rule can be extracted; the source is silent rather than explicitly denying stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialectal: the Kandi dialect has no top tone (replaced by high; fn. 4 p. 83, fn. 8 p. 86). Rising tone occurs only in a few morphemes, never in noun or verb stems; falling tone in a few verb stems (p. 86). Sentence-final tone lowering (high -> mid after low) is not marked in the paper's transcriptions except in sec. 2.1 (p. 87).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone contrasts are exemplified in phrases and sentences as well as citation forms; word division is stated to be arbitrary (fn. 7 p. 86) and several tone alternations are conditioned at sentence end, so the description operates at the phrase level as much as the word level. Nikki-Parakou dialect, fieldwork at Nikki, Dahomey, 1949.
new_statements.identity_note: Welmers 1952 describes the Nikki-Parakou dialect (fieldwork Nikki, Dahomey, 1949), which he reports as the prestige variety chosen for the written standard; he notes the Kandi dialect lacks the top tone. Glottolog baat1238 lists no dialect subdivisions, so the statement is taken as applying to the language-level entry. Names in the source: Bariba, Batonu /batɔnu/.

new_statements.quote: [p. 127, §7] Tonhöhe. 7. Sie wird in gleicher Weise wie in den oben erwähnten Arbeiten über die Mossi- und Grussi-Sprachengruppe bezeichnet. Ein Starkton ruht stets auf der Stammsilbe. Ko. hat offenbar durchweg den Starkton bezeichnet, denn bei ihm trägt die Stammsilbe in der Regel einen Akut. [Vorwort p. 2] In allen Sprachen ist die Beobachtung der Tonhöhen unerläßlich. Sie werden wie folgt bezeichnet: à ist a mit Tiefton, á Hochton, a̍ Mittelton, â Hochtiefton, ǎ Tiefhochton.
new_statements.translation: [p. 127, §7] Pitch. 7. It is marked in the same way as in the above-mentioned works on the Mossi and Grussi language groups. A stress accent (Starkton) always rests on the stem syllable. Ko[elle] has evidently marked the stress throughout, for with him the stem syllable as a rule carries an acute. [Preface p. 2] In all the languages the observation of the pitches is indispensable. They are marked as follows: à is a with low tone, á high tone, a̍ mid tone, â high-low (falling) tone, ǎ low-high (rising) tone.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Welmers 1952: tone language, four level tones plus rare contours, no stress statement): Westermann also treats pitch as lexically relevant and marks tones on the Bargu forms, and ADDS a stress statement the catalog lacks — a Starkton fixed on the stem syllable (root stress). It does not contradict the tonal classification; it is an older (1907 data, 1922 print), thinner source than Welmers, based on one unnamed speaker, and Welmers 1952 (Nikki dialect) says nothing about stress either way. the compilers tentative worry ('stress accent and no tones') is resolved: §7 explicitly says Tonhöhe is notated, and the word list carries high/low marks.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Westermann (data from one Bargu speaker, Lome 1907, a few sessions) marks lexical pitch (high/low/mid/falling/rising) on Bargu forms as in his other Gur sketches and states, in the pitch paragraph, that a dynamic stress ('Starkton') always lies on the stem (root) syllable, i.e. morphologically determined root stress in a suffixing class language (noun = stem + class suffix, so in disyllabic nouns the stress is stem-initial); he reads Koelle's Polyglotta acute on the stem syllable as marking the same stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; 'stets' (always) on the stem syllable; Koelle's acute is on the stem syllable 'in der Regel' (as a rule).
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann's 'Bargu' = Koelle's 'Barba' = Bariba/Baatonum of central and western Borgu (he equates it with the speech of Nikki and surroundings per Koelle, p. 124 §3); data from a single Bargu man in Lome, autumn 1907, name and home town not recorded (p. 126 §5), supplemented with Koelle's Polyglotta 'Barba' forms marked 'Ko.'. Welmers 1952 (catalog source) describes the Nikki-Parakou dialect.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records Bariba as 'tonal' from Welmers 1952 (four level + two contour tones, no stress statement). Westermann 1922 is compatible on tone (he marks Tonhöhe for Bargu with the same five tone signs used for all languages in the volume, Vorwort p. 2) and ADDS a word-stress statement absent from Welmers: a Starkton always on the stem syllable (morphological/root stress, effectively stem-initial in stem+suffix words). No placement conflict with the catalog because the catalog has no placement; the type on record would change from 'tonal, no stress statement' to 'tonal with a stress statement (stem syllable)'. Caveat on weight: a one-sentence claim from thin 1907 data, partly inferred…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bargu (Bariba) is written with tone marks (low/high/mid/falling/rising, as in Westermann's Mossi and Grussi studies), and in addition a dynamic stress ('Starkton') always lies on the stem (root) syllable of the word; Westermann reads the acute accents in Koelle's 1854 'Barba' list as marks of this stem stress. Since Bargu nouns are stem + class suffix (pp. 127, 129 ff.), stem stress is in practice stress on the first (root) syllable before the suffix.
new_statements.exceptions: none listed; the only hedge is 'in der Regel' (as a rule) about Koelle's acute falling on the stem syllable. The author warns (p. 126 par. 5) that the material comes from a few sessions with a single unnamed Bargu man met in Lome in autumn 1907 and is incomplete.
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann's 'Bargu' = Koelle's 'Barba/Barbar' (Polyglotta Africana), the language of central and western Borgu around Nikki (pp. 124-126), i.e. Bariba/Baatonum (baat1238); he explicitly separates it from Boko-Busa (Mande). Data: one unnamed Bargu man interviewed in Lome, autumn 1907, for a few sessions only, supplemented by Koelle's Barba words (marked 'Ko.'). Dialect of the informant not determined by the author.

readall_conflicts: Potential conflict, unverified: the HTRC extracted-features vocabulary of Westermann 1922 p. 127 (Starkton, Akut, ruht, trägt, Stammsilbe) indicates that Westermann described a stress accent on the stem syllable for Bargu and recorded no tones, whereas Welmers 1952 (the catalog's existing statement, verified on page scan) analyses Bariba as a language with four level tonemes plus falling and rising, and says nothing about stress. Westermann worked from a single Bargu speaker met in Lomé (the p. 126 tokens include 'Gewährsmannes', 'Lome', 'Aufnahme', 'Herbst', '1907') and often wrote 'Starkton' for what later fieldworkers analysed as tone, so the two are more likely a change of analysis than two different dialects; the sentence itself has not been read. No contradiction. The catalog (Welmers 1952) classifies Bariba as tonal with no statement about stress; Westermann 1922 p. 127 §7 likewise notates lexical pitch on his Bargu material and in addition places a dynamic stress ('Starkton') always on the stem syllable. The two differ only in that Westermann makes a stress statement (root/stem-syllable stress) where Welmers is silent; type (tone language) is the same. Westermann's evidence is thin (one unnamed speaker met in Lome in 1907, a few sessions, western/central Borgu speech) and should be weighted below Welmers' 1949 Nikki fieldwork, but nothing on record speaks against stem-syllable prominence.
